extracted.intended_audience: agency lawyers, hearing officers, administrative officials, and practitioners in administrative law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on conduct, evidence, decisionmaking, and procedural requirements for agency adjudications under the Administrative Procedure Act (sections 7 and 8). Covers who may preside, powers and duties of presiding officers, evidence and record rules, notice/official notice, and requirements for initial/recommended/final decisions and submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may preside at hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: There shall preside at the taking of evidence (1) the agency, (2) one or more members of the body which comprises the agency or (3) one or more examiners appointed as provided in this Act; but nothing in this Act shall be deemed to supersede the conduct of specified classes of proceedings in whole or part by or before boards or other officers specially provided for by or designated pursuant to statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The last clause permits use of boards or officers specially provided for or designated pursuant to statute; a statutory provision authorizing designation of a class of officers suffices. Examples include joint hearings with State designees, joint Federal boards, quota review committees, and boards of employees. Where a member of the agency acts as presiding officer, certain disqualification rules (section 5(c)) do not apply; a statute requiring a particular board or officer to conduct hearings may supersede inconsistent general requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality of presiding officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The functions of all presiding officers and of officers participating in decisions in conformity with section 8 shall be conducted in an impartial manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presiding officers must conduct hearings strictly impartially rather than as representatives of investigative or prosecuting authorities, but retain authority and duty to ensure necessary evidence is adduced and to keep hearings orderly and efficient. They may question witnesses and encourage making a complete record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal and disqualification procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Any such officer may at any time withdraw if he deems himself disqualified; and, upon the filing in good faith of a timely and sufficient affidavit of personal bias or disqualification of any such officer, the agency shall determine the matter as a part of the record and decision in the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party may file a timely, sufficient affidavit of bias; the agency determines the matter and must make the proceedings and decision part of the case record. Agencies need not hold a hearing on every charge; insufficient affidavits may be dismissed summarily. If a court later finds bias, relief depends on whether the private party was prejudiced by the error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers of presiding officers (enumerated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers presiding at hearings shall have authority, subject to the published rules of the agency and within its powers, to (1) administer oaths and affirmations, (2) issue subpenas authorized by law, (3) rule upon offers of proof and receive relevant evidence, (4) take or cause depositions to be taken whenever the ends of justice would be served thereby, (5) regulate the course of the hearing, (6) hold conferences for the settlement or simplification of the issues by consent of the parties, (7) dispose of procedural requests or similar matters, (8) make decisions or recommend decisions in conformity with section 8, and (9) take any other action authorized by agency rule consistent with this Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These powers are vested in hearing officers to the extent the agency itself possesses them—section 7(b) does not confer new substantive powers on the agency. Agencies cannot withhold these powers from hearing officers. The phrase 'subject to the published rules of the agency' preserves the agency's ability to prescribe policies and procedural rules governing the exercise of these powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency rules govern exercise of presiding powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'subject to the published rules of the agency' is intended to make clear the authority of the agency to lay down policies and procedural rules which will govern the exercise of such powers by presiding officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: if agency rule prescribes a manner to establish citizenship, the hearing officer must conform when ruling on offers of proof; subpoenas duces tecum may be constrained by agency rules specifying written application and relevance. Agencies may provide for appeals to the agency head from hearing officer rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency appeal from hearing officer rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies remain free to provide for appeals to the agency heads from rulings of hearing officers in the exercise of the powers enumerated in section 7(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate appeals may be desirable in instances where reversal would require reopening the hearing and recalling witnesses. Agencies should decide and publish procedures for appeals from rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as statutes otherwise provide, the proponent of a rule or order shall have the burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'burden of proof' is used largely as synonymous with the 'burden of going forward' rather than in a strict evidentiary sense. Specific statutes that establish presumptions or otherwise alter burdens are not repealed by this general rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and exclusion of evidence; standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Any oral or documentary evidence may be received, but every agency shall as a matter of policy provide for the exclusion of irrelevant, immaterial, or unduly repetitious evidence and no sanction shall be imposed or rule or order be issued except upon consideration of the whole record or such portions thereof as may be cited by any party and as supported by and in accordance with the reliable, probative, and substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical rules of evidence do not apply to administrative hearings; mere admission of evidence is not prejudicial error. Agencies should direct hearing officers to exclude irrelevant, immaterial, or unduly repetitious evidence for efficiency and good practice. Judicial review continues under the 'substantial evidence' standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nontechnical evidence regime (hearsay, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The technical rules of evidence will not be applicable to administrative hearings; the mere admission of evidence is not to be taken as prejudicial error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although hearsay and other nontechnical evidence may be admitted, agencies should exclude irrelevant or unduly repetitious material. Agencies may impose reasonable requirements as to how particular facts must be established and draw inferences or presumptions customary in courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency authority to require methods of proof and draw inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in section 7(c) is intended to preclude an agency from imposing reasonable requirements as to how particular facts must be established nor to forbid customary inferences or presumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may require specified methods to establish age, citizenship, marital status, etc., and may rely on inferences like failure to explain by a party in exclusive possession of the facts or presumption of continuity once shown. Section 7(c) does not repeal statutory presumptions elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to present case and cross-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Every party shall have the right to present his case or defense by oral or documentary evidence, to submit rebuttal evidence, and to conduct such cross-examination as may be required for a full and true disclosure of the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This emphasizes the right in adjudication to present oral evidence and documentary evidence admissible in judicial proceedings (e.g., business records). 'Documentary evidence' does not mean affidavits or written evidence of any kind; agencies may receive written evidence only when admission will not prejudicially deprive other parties of opportunity for cross‑examination. Technical/statistical data may be introduced in written form subject to cross‑examination and rebuttal opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on affidavits and written evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to present case by oral or documentary evidence does not extend to presenting evidence in affidavit or other written form so as to deprive the agency or opposing parties of opportunity for cross-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admission of affidavits as a substitute for live testimony is disfavored because it could flood proceedings with hearsay and deprive parties of cross‑examination. Agencies may, however, receive written evidence when it is reliable and probative and does not prejudicially deprive parties of cross‑examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limitation of cross-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The provision for 'such cross-examination as may be required for a full and true disclosure of the facts' does not confer a right of 'unlimited' cross-examination; presiding officers must determine whether cross-examination is pressed to unreasonable lengths or is required for a full and true disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presiding officers have discretion to curtail cross-examination when it adds nothing substantial to the record or would unduly prolong hearings, particularly in rulemaking or broadly economic/statistical matters with numerous parties or witnesses. Where cross-examination is necessary to bring out the truth, it should be allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-evidence procedures in rulemaking, rate‑making, and benefits determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: In proceedings involving rule making or determining claims for money or benefits or applications for initial licenses, an agency may adopt procedures for the submission of all or part of the evidence in written form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedures may be required only where the interest of any party will not be prejudiced thereby—typical where veracity and demeanor of witnesses are unimportant. Agencies routinely use written evidence procedures to simplify records and shorten hearings; sufficient opportunity for rebuttal must exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record for decision and its contents
rubrics_metrics.description: The transcript of testimony and exhibits, together with all papers and requests filed in the proceeding, shall constitute the exclusive record for decision in accordance with section 8 and, upon payment of lawfully prescribed costs, shall be made available to the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record must include proceedings on affidavits of bias; all decisions (initial, recommended, or tentative) must be part of the record. Agencies need not transcribe automatically in every case but must transcribe when a party requests a copy (upon payment). Practices like contracting with private reporting services to allow parties to obtain copies at reasonable price satisfy the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official notice of material facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where any agency decision rests on official notice of a material fact not appearing in the evidence in the record, any party shall on timely request be afforded an opportunity to show the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official notice may extend beyond traditional judicial notice to matters of technical or scientific fact within the agency's expertise. Matters noticed should be specified on the record or in the decision, and parties must be given opportunity to request reopening to contest officially noticed facts. Official notice may be taken at any stage, including the final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who makes initial, recommended, tentative, and final decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases in which the agency has not presided at the reception of the evidence, the officer who presided shall initially decide the case or the agency shall require the entire record to be certified to it for initial decision; when the agency makes the initial decision without having presided, such officers shall first recommend a decision; the agency may issue tentative decisions or omit intermediate procedures in specified cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 8(a) bridges the gap between hearing officials and deciding officials. Agencies should determine whether presiding officers' decisions will be 'initial' (become agency decision if not appealed) or 'recommended'. In rulemaking and initial-license proceedings, agencies may issue tentative decisions or follow staff reports rather than examiner recommendations; agencies may find on the record that they must decide directly to meet exigent needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of initial decisions and appeals to agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever such officers make the initial decision and in the absence of either an appeal to the agency or review upon motion of the agency within time provided by rule, such decision shall without further proceedings then become the decision of the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may appeal hearing officer initial decisions to the agency; the agency may also review initial decisions sua sponte. Agencies should publish rules prescribing appeal/review time limits. Agencies may require appeal to agency as a prerequisite to judicial review if set forth in published rule (and may make the hearing officer's initial decision inoperative pending review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency review powers and limitations on review issues
rubrics_metrics.description: On appeal from or review of the initial decisions of such officers the agency shall, except as it may limit the issues upon notice or by rule, have all the powers which it would have in making the initial decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agency is not bound by subordinate decisions and may consider all matters anew. However, the agency may limit issues for review by notice or rule (e.g., to questions of law and policy or to alleged clear errors of fact). Agencies may require precise, record‑supported exceptions and may limit consideration to issues properly presented as exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency disposition options on review
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency may adopt in whole or in part the findings, conclusions and basis stated by the presiding officer; it may make entirely new findings on the record or on new evidence; or it may remand the case to the hearing officer for further proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies have broad discretion— they may attach weight to examiner credibility findings (especially when demeanor matters) but may also reopen or take new evidence where appropriate. Remand and new findings are permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to submit proposed findings, exceptions, and supporting reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to each recommended, initial, or tentative decision, or decision upon agency review of the decision of subordinate officers, the parties shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to submit for the consideration of the officers participating in such decisions (1) proposed findings and conclusions, or (2) exceptions to the decisions or recommended decisions of subordinate officers or to tentative agency decisions, and (3) supporting reasons for such exceptions or proposed findings or conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This codifies existing practice to focus issues and arguments. Agencies may require proposed findings, conclusions and exceptions to be supported by precise citations to the record or legal authorities and may impose reasonable time limits. Briefs on law and facts must be received and considered. Section 8(b) does not mandate oral argument; agencies decide when oral argument is necessary or appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and form requirements for decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: All decisions (including initial, recommended, or tentative decisions) shall become a part of the record and include a statement of (1) findings and conclusions, as well as the reasons or basis therefor, upon all the material issues of fact, law, or discretion presented on the record; and (2) the appropriate rule, order, sanction, relief, or denial thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions must indicate the ruling upon each requested finding, conclusion, or exception to preclude later controversy about what the agency did. The requirement that reasons be stated ensures transparency and allows meaningful review; agencies may adopt findings of subordinates or formulate new findings but must record the basis for material determinations.
